47	**[Section 1: Engagement Overview and Scope]{.underline}**
48	
49	Hartwell & Stein LLP (\"Hartwell & Stein\" or \"we\") was retained by Ridgeline Therapeutics, Inc. (\"Ridgeline\" or the \"Company\") to prepare a transfer pricing benchmarking study analyzing the arm\'s-length royalty rate applicable to the license of oncology drug portfolio intellectual property from Ridgeline (the \"Licensor\") to Ridgeline Therapeutics Ireland Ltd. (\"RTIL\") (the \"Licensee\") under a License Agreement dated 2016 (the \"2016 License Agreement\"). The engagement was initiated by the Company\'s tax department and was supervised throughout by Ridgeline\'s Tax Director, Sandra Kwon.
50	
51	Ridgeline is a Delaware C-corporation, publicly traded on NASDAQ under the ticker symbol RDGL, with its principal executive offices located at 400 Cascade Boulevard, Suite 1200, San Diego, California 92130. Ridgeline\'s Employer Identification Number (EIN) is 47-3918205. Ridgeline is principally engaged in the research, development, manufacturing, and commercialization of proprietary oncology therapeutics.
52	
53	RTIL is an Irish private limited company with a registered office at 25 St. Stephen\'s Green, Dublin 2, Ireland. RTIL is a wholly owned subsidiary of Ridgeline and serves as the Company\'s primary operating entity for the manufacture, marketing, and distribution of licensed oncology products in territories outside the United States.
54	
55	We note the existence of additional controlled entities within the Ridgeline group, including Ridgeline Asia-Pacific Pte. Ltd., organized in Singapore, and Ridgeline Pharma GmbH, organized in Zug, Switzerland. These entities are not parties to the 2016 License Agreement and their intercompany transactions are outside the scope of this study.
56	
57	This benchmarking study was originally prepared as of November 15, 2018, covering the projected royalty economics under the 2016 License Agreement based on available financial data and forward-looking revenue projections at that time. An addendum was subsequently prepared in March 2022 to incorporate actual financial data for fiscal years 2019 through 2021 and preliminary financial data for fiscal year 2022. Both the original study and the March 2022 addendum were completed prior to the filing of Ridgeline\'s federal income tax returns for the respective tax years under examination.
58	
59	The scope of this study is to determine whether the 12% net-sales-based royalty rate established in the 2016 License Agreement between Ridgeline and RTIL satisfies the arm\'s-length standard under Section 482 of the Internal Revenue Code (\"IRC §482\") and the corresponding Treasury Regulations (Treas. Reg. §1.482-1 through §1.482-9), with specific focus on the arm\'s-length range for royalty rates in comparable licensing transactions involving pharmaceutical intellectual property.
60	
61	The purpose of this study is to serve as contemporaneous documentation under Treas. Reg. §1.6662-6(d), establishing that Ridgeline made a reasonable effort to determine and apply an arm\'s-length price for the intercompany royalty transaction, thereby supporting a reasonable cause and good faith defense under IRC §6664(c) should the Internal Revenue Service challenge the intercompany pricing.
62	
63	This executive summary is prepared for the benefit of Ridgeline\'s management, including Sandra Kwon (Tax Director), Jonathan Hess (Chief Financial Officer), Raj Patel (Vice President of International Tax), and Meredith Colton (General Counsel), as well as Ridgeline\'s outside tax counsel at Pemberton Hale & Griggs LLP, specifically Eleanor Marsh (Partner) and David Yun (Senior Associate).
64	
65	**[Section 2: Description of the Controlled Transaction]{.underline}**
66	
67	Under the 2016 License Agreement, Ridgeline granted RTIL an exclusive license to manufacture, market, and distribute Ridgeline\'s proprietary oncology drug portfolio in all territories outside the United States (the \"Licensed Territory\"). The licensed intellectual property (the \"Licensed IP\") encompasses patents, trade secrets, clinical data, regulatory filings, manufacturing process know-how, and associated proprietary information related to Ridgeline\'s oncology therapeutic compounds. Ridgeline retained all rights to manufacture, market, and distribute the licensed products within the United States market.
68	
69	The compensation structure under the 2016 License Agreement provides that RTIL pays Ridgeline a running royalty equal to 12% of net sales of licensed products. For purposes of the agreement, \"net sales\" is defined as gross sales of licensed products in the Licensed Territory less returns, rebates, chargebacks, and distribution fees. No upfront license fees or milestone payments are included in the compensation structure; the 12% running royalty is the sole form of intercompany compensation for the licensed intellectual property.
70	
71	The following table presents RTIL\'s net sales of licensed products and corresponding royalty payments for the tax years under examination:
72	
73	  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
74	  **Fiscal Year**   **RTIL Net Sales (USD millions)**   **Royalty Rate**   **Royalty Paid to Ridgeline (USD millions)**
75	  ----------------- ----------------------------------- ------------------ ----------------------------------------------
76	  2019              \$412.0                             12%                \$49.44
77	
78	  2020              \$587.0                             12%                \$70.44
79	
80	  2021              \$734.0                             12%                \$88.08
81	
82	  2022              \$891.0                             12%                \$106.92
83	
84	  **Total**         **\$2,624.0**                       ---                **\$314.88**
85	  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
86	
87	RTIL performs meaningful and substantive functions in connection with the licensed products. RTIL bears manufacturing risk through oversight of contract manufacturing arrangements for the Licensed Territory, regulatory risk through its management of European Medicines Agency (\"EMA\") and national regulatory authority filings and compliance, commercial risk through marketing, distribution, and market access activities, and inventory risk through management of finished goods inventory for distribution. As of the most recent data available, RTIL employed approximately 180 personnel in Dublin, including staff in regulatory affairs, medical affairs, commercial operations, supply chain management, and market access functions.
88	
89	Ridgeline, as the U.S. parent and IP owner, developed the Licensed IP through extensive research and development activities, continues to bear ongoing R&D risk for pipeline compounds and next-generation formulations, and funds the majority of clinical development programs. Ridgeline maintains a research workforce of over 600 scientists and clinical development professionals at its San Diego headquarters. Ridgeline\'s consolidated revenue for fiscal year 2022 was approximately \$1.87 billion.
90	
91	Based on our functional analysis, we conclude that Ridgeline owns the high-value intangible assets and performs the critical Development, Enhancement, Maintenance, Protection, and Exploitation (\"DEMPE\") functions as contemplated by the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines. RTIL functions as the licensed distributor and manufacturer for the ex-US territory, bearing routine-to-moderate entrepreneurial risk commensurate with its operational activities and local market responsibilities. This functional characterization is central to the selection of the appropriate transfer pricing method and the identification of reliable comparable transactions.
92	
93	**[Section 3: Selection of Transfer Pricing Method]{.underline}**
94	
95	In selecting the transfer pricing method most appropriate for evaluating the arm\'s-length nature of the 12% royalty rate, we applied the \"best method\" rule under Treas. Reg. §1.482-1(c), which requires that the method selected provide the most reliable measure of an arm\'s-length result given the facts and circumstances of the controlled transaction. We also considered the guidance set forth in Treas. Reg. §1.482-4(a) regarding the pricing of transfers of intangible property. We evaluated the following methods:
96	
97	**1. Comparable Uncontrolled Transaction (CUT) Method (Treas. Reg. §1.482-4(c)):** The CUT method evaluates whether the royalty charged in a controlled transaction is arm\'s-length by reference to the royalty charged in comparable uncontrolled transactions. Pharmaceutical intellectual property licensing transactions are sufficiently common in the public domain --- through license agreements filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, disclosed in merger and acquisition proxy statements, and compiled in proprietary licensing databases --- to identify comparable uncontrolled royalty arrangements. Given the availability of reliable comparable data and the direct correspondence between the tested transaction (a royalty license) and the comparable transactions (third-party royalty licenses), we selected the CUT method as the best method for this analysis.
98	
99	**2. Comparable Profits Method (CPM) (Treas. Reg. §1.482-5):** The CPM evaluates whether the operating results of a controlled taxpayer are consistent with the operating results of comparable uncontrolled taxpayers. While CPM could be applied to test RTIL\'s profitability against that of comparable distributors or manufacturers, we concluded that the CUT method provides a more direct and reliable measure of the arm\'s-length royalty rate because the controlled transaction is explicitly structured as a royalty license. The CPM would measure the arm\'s-length result only indirectly, by reference to RTIL\'s overall profitability rather than the specific royalty rate. Accordingly, we rejected CPM as a secondary method.
100	
101	**3. Profit Split Method (PSM) (Treas. Reg. §1.482-6):** The PSM allocates the combined operating profit from a controlled transaction between the parties based on their relative contributions to value creation. While both Ridgeline and RTIL contribute to value creation, the arrangement is structured as a license agreement with a defined royalty compensation mechanism, not as a joint venture or cost-sharing arrangement. Application of the PSM would require significant assumptions regarding the allocation of combined profits, introducing a degree of analytical uncertainty that is avoidable through the more direct CUT approach. We therefore rejected PSM.
102	
103	Our selection of the CUT method is consistent with the guidance in the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises and Tax Administrations, particularly Chapter VI (Special Considerations for Intangibles) and Chapter II (Transfer Pricing Methods). The CUT method is widely recognized as the most reliable method where sufficiently comparable uncontrolled transactions involving similar intangible property can be identified.
104	
105	We note that Treas. Reg. §1.482-4(c)(2) requires that the comparable uncontrolled transactions involve sufficiently similar intangible property and contractual terms, with adjustments for material differences in comparability factors. Our comparability analysis and adjustments are described in Sections 4 and 5 below.
106	
107	**[Section 4: Comparables Search and Selection Process]{.underline}**
108	
109	To identify comparable uncontrolled transactions for purposes of the CUT analysis, we conducted a comprehensive search of multiple licensing databases, regulatory filings, and publicly available transaction data. Our search encompassed oncology-related intellectual property licensing agreements executed between 2012 and 2018 (with the March 2022 addendum extending the search window to agreements executed through 2021). Sources included publicly filed license agreements available through the SEC\'s EDGAR database, disclosed licensing terms in pharmaceutical company annual reports (Form 10-K), quarterly reports (Form 10-Q), and investor presentations, as well as proprietary licensing agreement databases maintained by Hartwell & Stein LLP, which compile licensing terms from publicly available sources.
110	
111	Our initial search identified a universe of 147 licensing agreements involving pharmaceutical intellectual property in oncology or closely related therapeutic areas. We applied the following sequential screening criteria to narrow the comparables set to the most reliable and relevant transactions:
112	
113	**Step 1 --- Therapeutic Area:** We retained only licensing agreements involving oncology and immuno-oncology compounds, eliminating agreements for unrelated therapeutic areas (e.g., cardiovascular, neurology, metabolic disease). This reduced the universe to 89 agreements.
114	
115	**Step 2 --- Transaction Type:** We retained only outbound licenses from an IP owner to a licensee for manufacturing and distribution rights, eliminating co-development agreements, co-promotion arrangements, and technology platform licenses where the economic substance differed materially from the controlled transaction. This reduced the set to 54 agreements.
116	
117	**Step 3 --- Stage of Development:** We retained only licenses involving compounds at Phase III clinical stage or commercial stage, eliminating agreements for early-stage, preclinical, Phase I, or Phase II compounds. The rationale for this criterion is that royalty rates for early-stage compounds reflect significantly different risk profiles and expected value relative to late-stage or commercial-stage compounds comparable to Ridgeline\'s licensed portfolio. This reduced the set to 31 agreements.
118	
119	**Step 4 --- Royalty Structure:** We retained only agreements with royalties based on a percentage of net sales, eliminating milestone-only arrangements, fixed-fee structures, and hybrid arrangements where the royalty component could not be reliably isolated from other forms of consideration. This reduced the set to 22 agreements.
120	
121	**Step 5 --- Territorial Scope:** We retained only agreements involving ex-US or multi-territory rights comparable to RTIL\'s license scope under the 2016 License Agreement, eliminating US-only licenses that do not reflect the economic characteristics of the Licensed Territory. This reduced the set to 16 agreements.
122	
123	**Step 6 --- Related-Party Exclusion:** We eliminated any transactions between known related parties, as such transactions may not reflect arm\'s-length pricing. This reduced the set to 15 agreements.
124	
125	**Step 7 --- Data Sufficiency:** We eliminated agreements where the royalty rate was redacted, not publicly available, or otherwise insufficiently documented to permit reliable analysis. This final screening step yielded the **final comparable set of 12 agreements**.
126	
127	The 12 comparable transactions involve the licensing of commercial-stage oncology compounds for ex-US territories, with royalties expressed as a percentage of net sales --- the same compensation structure as the controlled transaction. The identities of the specific comparable companies and agreements, together with detailed descriptions of the comparable transactions, are provided in Appendix C of the Full Report. This executive summary presents aggregated results only.
128	
129	**[Section 5: Comparability Adjustments]{.underline}**
130	
131	Consistent with the requirements of Treas. Reg. §1.482-4(c)(2), we applied both qualitative and quantitative comparability adjustments to enhance the reliability of the CUT analysis. The regulations recognize that perfect comparability is rarely achievable and that adjustments for material differences between the controlled transaction and the comparable uncontrolled transactions are appropriate and expected.
132	
133	We analyzed the following comparability factors for each of the 12 comparable transactions:
134	
135	**1. Nature of the Intangible:** All 12 comparable transactions involve patented pharmaceutical compounds in oncology, providing a strong baseline of comparability with the Licensed IP. Within this set, we made adjustments for differences in remaining market exclusivity (patent life), breadth of approved and pipeline indications, and competitive positioning within the respective oncology sub-segments. Compounds with longer remaining patent protection or broader indication coverage generally commanded higher royalty rates.
136	
137	**2. Contractual Terms:** We analyzed and adjusted for differences in license exclusivity (all 12 comparables were exclusive licenses, consistent with the controlled transaction), sublicensing rights, license duration, and termination provisions. Agreements with more restrictive sublicensing rights or shorter durations were adjusted upward to reflect the relatively more favorable terms available to RTIL under the 2016 License Agreement.
138	
139	**3. Functions and Risks of the Licensee:** Adjustments were made for differences in the extent of manufacturing responsibility assumed by the licensee (certain comparables involved licensees that outsourced all manufacturing, while RTIL maintains contract manufacturing oversight), regulatory responsibility, and the scale of commercial infrastructure required. Licensees bearing greater functional responsibility typically negotiated lower royalty rates, reflecting their greater contribution to post-license value creation.
140	
141	**4. Geographic Territory:** We adjusted for differences in the territorial scope of the comparable licenses relative to the controlled transaction. Certain comparables covered Europe-only territories, while others encompassed global ex-US rights including emerging markets. Broader territorial grants generally corresponded to higher royalty rates, reflecting greater revenue potential.
142	
143	**5. Volume and Growth Trajectory:** We made adjustments to account for differences in the scale of net sales and growth expectations at the time of the respective license agreements. Transactions involving larger anticipated revenue bases in some instances reflected lower per-unit royalty rates due to volume effects.
144	
145	Where quantitative adjustments were feasible --- for example, territory scope adjustments based on proportional revenue potential --- they were applied directly to the reported royalty rates. Where only qualitative assessments were supportable given available data, they were noted and considered in the determination of the arm\'s-length range. Detailed calculations supporting each adjustment are provided in Appendix D of the Full Report.
146	
147	After application of these adjustments, the 12 comparable transactions yielded adjusted royalty rates suitable for the interquartile range analysis presented in Section 6.
148	
149	**[Section 6: Results --- Arm\'s-Length Range]{.underline}**
150	
151	The following table presents the distribution of adjusted royalty rates derived from the 12 comparable uncontrolled transactions after application of the comparability adjustments described in Section 5:
152	
153	  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
154	  **Statistical Measure**             **Adjusted Royalty Rate (% of Net Sales)**
155	  ----------------------------------- --------------------------------------------
156	  Minimum                             8.0%
157	
158	  25th Percentile (Q1)                **10.5%**
159	
160	  Median                              **13.5%**
161	
162	  75th Percentile (Q3)                **16.8%**
163	
164	  Maximum                             21.0%
165	  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
166	
167	The **interquartile range (\"IQR\") of arm\'s-length royalty rates is 10.5% to 16.8%** of net sales.
168	
169	Under Treas. Reg. §1.482-1(e)(2)(iii)(B), where the results of a controlled transaction fall within the interquartile range of results derived from comparable uncontrolled transactions, the controlled transaction is generally considered to produce an arm\'s-length result, and the Internal Revenue Service should not make an allocation under IRC §482. The interquartile range represents the zone of arm\'s-length outcomes that accounts for residual imprecision in comparability, reflecting the range within which independent parties operating under similar conditions and circumstances would be expected to transact.
170	
171	**The 12% royalty rate established in the 2016 License Agreement between Ridgeline and RTIL falls within the interquartile range of 10.5% to 16.8%.** Specifically, the 12% rate falls between the 25th percentile (10.5%) and the median (13.5%) of the comparable set. The royalty rate is therefore consistent with an arm\'s-length result under the CUT method analysis.
172	
173	The median royalty rate of 13.5% suggests that the 12% rate is modestly below the central tendency of the comparable set. This positioning is economically rational and consistent with the functional analysis: RTIL makes meaningful contributions to the commercialization of the licensed products through its commercial infrastructure, regulatory capabilities, and assumption of local market risk, functions that justify a royalty rate below the median as RTIL retains a share of profits commensurate with its risk and functional contributions.
174	
175	**Sensitivity Analysis:** To test the robustness of our conclusions, we conducted a sensitivity analysis using a narrower subset of the 8 most closely comparable transactions (i.e., those requiring the fewest and smallest comparability adjustments). Under this more conservative analysis, the interquartile range was 11.0% to 17.2%, with a median of 14.0%. The 12% royalty rate remains within this narrower IQR, further confirming the arm\'s-length character of the controlled transaction.
176	
177	We note for context that the IRS Revenue Agent assigned to Ridgeline\'s examination, Michael Salgado (Badge No. 74-06133), proposed a royalty rate of 19.5% in the Revenue Agent\'s Report. This proposed rate exceeds not only the 75th percentile (16.8%) of our primary comparables set but also the 75th percentile (17.2%) of the narrowed sensitivity set. While the maximum observed rate in the full comparable sample was 21.0%, rates at the extremes of the distribution reflect transactions with materially different risk profiles, IP characteristics, or contractual terms and are not representative of the arm\'s-length standard under the best-method analysis. The 19.5% proposed rate does not, in our professional judgment, reflect an arm\'s-length outcome for a transaction with the characteristics of the 2016 License Agreement.
178	
179	We further note that the settlement rate of 16% negotiated through IRS Appeals (Appeals Team Case Leader Patricia Voss, Badge No. 74-02891) falls just below the 75th percentile of the IQR and is consistent with the upper end of the arm\'s-length range. A rate at this level is within the range of outcomes that independent parties could reasonably agree upon, though it reflects a less favorable positioning for the licensee than the originally agreed 12% rate.
180	
181	**[Section 7: Reasonable Cause and Contemporaneous Documentation Defense]{.underline}**
182	
183	Under IRC §6662(e), an accuracy-related penalty of 20% (or 40% in the case of a gross valuation misstatement) may be imposed on the underpayment of tax attributable to a transfer pricing adjustment that results in a substantial valuation misstatement or gross valuation misstatement. These penalties can be significant, particularly in high-value intercompany transactions such as the royalty arrangement between Ridgeline and RTIL.
184	
185	However, IRC §6664(c)(1) provides that no penalty shall be imposed under §6662 with respect to any portion of an underpayment if the taxpayer demonstrates that there was reasonable cause for the position taken and that the taxpayer acted in good faith.
186	
187	Treas. Reg. §1.6662-6(d) specifies the requirements for establishing a reasonable cause defense in the transfer pricing context. A taxpayer may satisfy these requirements by demonstrating that it maintained \"contemporaneous documentation\" --- defined as transfer pricing documentation that was in existence at the time the relevant tax return was filed --- meeting the specific requirements set forth in Treas. Reg. §1.6662-6(d)(2)(iii). These requirements include:
188	
189	> \(a\) a description of the principal documents relied upon in the analysis;
190	>
191	> \(b\) a description of the transfer pricing method selected and the reasons for selecting that method;
192	>
193	> \(c\) identification and description of comparable transactions used in the analysis;
194	>
195	> \(d\) a description of comparability adjustments applied; and
196	>
197	> \(e\) a statement explaining why the controlled transaction produces results consistent with the arm\'s-length standard.
198	
199	This benchmarking study satisfies each of these requirements. Sections 2 through 6 of this executive summary, and the corresponding sections of the Full Report, contain detailed descriptions of the principal documents, the selected method and rationale, the comparable transactions, the comparability adjustments, and the economic basis for concluding that the 12% royalty rate produces arm\'s-length results.
200	
201	Critically, **this benchmarking study was originally prepared on November 15, 2018** --- well in advance of the filing of Ridgeline\'s federal income tax return for the 2019 tax year and substantially before the Internal Revenue Service commenced its examination of Ridgeline\'s returns on March 15, 2023. **The addendum dated March 2022** updated the analysis to incorporate actual financial data through fiscal year 2021 and preliminary data for fiscal year 2022. Both the original study and the addendum were completed before the filing of the respective tax returns for the years covered by each document.
202	
203	Accordingly, Ridgeline maintained contemporaneous documentation as defined by Treas. Reg. §1.6662-6(d)(2)(iii) for each of the tax years 2019 through 2022, which are the years under examination.
204	
205	Additionally, Ridgeline\'s management relied in good faith on the analysis performed by qualified transfer pricing economists. The lead economist on this engagement, Dr. Nathan Foley, is a recognized expert in pharmaceutical transfer pricing with extensive experience in CUT analyses for biotechnology and pharmaceutical intellectual property transactions. His curriculum vitae is included as Appendix F to the Full Report. Ridgeline also relied on the counsel of its outside tax advisors at Pemberton Hale & Griggs LLP, specifically Eleanor Marsh (Partner, Cal. Bar No. 198244), who advised on the regulatory requirements for contemporaneous documentation and the application of the arm\'s-length standard.
206	
207	Based on the foregoing, it is our conclusion that Ridgeline has a strong reasonable cause defense under IRC §6664(c) and Treas. Reg. §1.6662-6(d) for all examined tax years (2019--2022), supporting full abatement of any accuracy-related penalty under IRC §6662(e) related to the transfer pricing adjustment proposed by the IRS.
208	
209	**[Section 8: Conclusions and Recommendations]{.underline}**
210	
211	**Primary Conclusion:** The 12% royalty rate under the 2016 License Agreement between Ridgeline Therapeutics, Inc. and Ridgeline Therapeutics Ireland Ltd. is within the arm\'s-length interquartile range of 10.5% to 16.8% determined through application of the Comparable Uncontrolled Transaction method. The royalty rate therefore satisfies the arm\'s-length standard under IRC §482 and Treas. Reg. §1.482-4.
212	
213	**Secondary Conclusion:** The contemporaneous nature of this documentation --- originally prepared November 15, 2018, with an addendum prepared in March 2022 --- combined with the rigorous methodology and qualified expertise applied in its preparation, supports a reasonable cause and good faith defense under IRC §6664(c) for all tax years 2019 through 2022.
214	
215	Based on our analysis, we offer the following recommendations:
216	
217	**Recommendation 1:** Ridgeline should continue to maintain and annually update its transfer pricing documentation to ensure contemporaneous documentation coverage for future tax years. Annual updates should incorporate the most recent available financial data, any changes to the functional profiles of the parties, and any new comparable transactions identified through ongoing database monitoring. Hartwell & Stein LLP stands ready to prepare such annual updates upon request.
218	
219	**Recommendation 2:** Ridgeline should recognize that the arm\'s-length range represents a zone of reasonable outcomes, not a single point estimate. Should the IRS challenge the 12% rate, any adjustment that sets the royalty rate within the IQR of 10.5% to 16.8% would itself be consistent with arm\'s-length principles under the applicable regulations. Ridgeline may wish to consider the strategic implications of where within the range the Company\'s pricing falls in the context of potential examination risk and settlement negotiations.
220	
221	**Recommendation 3:** Ridgeline should retain all underlying data, work papers, comparable transaction analyses, and source materials for the benchmarking study for at least the period of the applicable statute of limitations. Under IRC §6501(a), the general limitations period is three years from the date the return was filed; however, under IRC §6501(e), this period may be extended to six years in cases involving substantial omissions of gross income. Ridgeline should consult with its legal counsel regarding the appropriate retention period in light of the ongoing examination and any extensions of the statute of limitations that may have been executed.
222	
223	**[Section 9: Limitations and Disclaimers]{.underline}**
224	
225	This executive summary is prepared solely for the use of Ridgeline Therapeutics, Inc. and its authorized advisors, including Pemberton Hale & Griggs LLP (outside tax counsel) and Pinnacle Accounting Group LLP (external auditor). It is not intended for distribution to, or reliance by, any third party without the prior written consent of Hartwell & Stein LLP. Any third party that obtains access to this document does so at its own risk, and Hartwell & Stein LLP assumes no responsibility or liability to any such third party.
226	
227	The conclusions contained herein are based on the facts, data, and economic conditions available as of the date of the original report (November 15, 2018) and the March 2022 addendum. Changes in market conditions, regulatory environments, competitive dynamics, or the landscape of comparable licensing transactions could affect the results of the analysis. The conclusions should not be extrapolated to periods beyond the scope of the analysis without further study.
228	
229	Hartwell & Stein LLP has relied on financial data and factual representations provided by Ridgeline\'s management, including RTIL net sales figures, functional descriptions, employee headcount data, and contractual terms of the 2016 License Agreement. Hartwell & Stein LLP has not independently audited or verified this data. Ridgeline\'s external auditor, Pinnacle Accounting Group LLP (Engagement Partner: Lisa Takahashi, CPA), has audited Ridgeline\'s consolidated financial statements for the relevant periods, and the financial data used in this study is consistent with the audited financials as reported in Ridgeline\'s Annual Reports on Form 10-K filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission.
230	
231	This study does not constitute legal advice or a legal opinion on the ultimate outcome of any IRS examination, administrative proceeding, or litigation. The interpretation and application of tax law is the province of Ridgeline\'s legal counsel, and Ridgeline should rely on the advice of Pemberton Hale & Griggs LLP for all matters requiring legal judgment.
232	
233	The scope of this study is limited to the intercompany royalty transaction between Ridgeline and RTIL under the 2016 License Agreement. This study does not analyze, and no conclusions should be drawn regarding, any other intercompany transactions within the Ridgeline group, including but not limited to transactions involving Ridgeline Asia-Pacific Pte. Ltd. (Singapore) or Ridgeline Pharma GmbH (Zug, Switzerland).
234	
235	This study does not address state, local, or foreign tax implications of the intercompany royalty arrangement. The analysis is limited to the application of the arm\'s-length standard under IRC §482 and the corresponding Treasury Regulations for United States federal income tax purposes.
236	
237	**[Certification]{.underline}**
238	
239	Respectfully submitted,
240

248	
249	I certify that the analysis, conclusions, and recommendations contained in this report are based on my independent professional judgment, applied in accordance with generally accepted transfer pricing economic principles. This report was prepared in accordance with the applicable transfer pricing regulations under IRC §482 and the Treasury Regulations thereunder, as well as the relevant professional standards governing economic analyses of this nature. Neither I nor Hartwell & Stein LLP have any financial interest in the outcome of this analysis beyond the professional fees received for the preparation of this study.
250	
251	**[Appendix References]{.underline}**
252	
253	The following appendices are contained in the Full Report and are incorporated by reference into this executive summary. These appendices are not reproduced herein.

dict(id="6", sev="High", cat="Interest", prov="Sections VII.A–VII.C; Exhibit C Line 4 and Footnote 2",
title="Interest of $3,740,000 is unsupported and appears materially understated, yet the draft fixes it as a “final determination”",
issue="(a) Appeals has twice declined to give a year-by-year computation (Nov. 22 and Dec. 18, 2024 emails), even though Ridgeline asked for one in writing on Nov. 14 and Dec. 5. dict(id="9", sev="High", cat="Substantive tax", prov="Sections VI.A–VI.D; Exhibit C Line 3",
title="FTC adjustment: no computation; the stated rationale conflicts with the sourcing rules; obsolete §902 reference; carryover treatment not addressed",
issue="(a) No computation supports the $2,310,000. The RAR left the FTC impact “TBD,” Ridgeline’s Nov. 14 email asked to “review and verify,” and Mr. Patel’s review was still open on Dec. 5. The only corroboration is Ridgeline’s own reserve sensitivity (16% scenario = $2,310,000), which rests on estimated limitations. (b) Sections VI.A and VI.C describe the incremental royalty as U.S.-source income. Royalties paid for the right to use intangibles outside the United States are foreign-source under §862(a)(4) (cf. §861(a)(4)), and RTIL uses the Licensed IP only outside the United States. Look-through under §904(d)(3) would generally place the royalty in the general category. On that analysis the adjustment increases foreign-source income in the general basket. Any reduction in allowable credits would arise elsewhere, for example through reduced RTIL tested income and §960(d) deemed-paid credits in the §951A basket, or through expense apportionment. The narrative and the dollar figure therefore need to be rebuilt from an actual computation. (c) Section VI.B invokes §902 “for tax years beginning before January 1, 2018”; every Covered Tax Year is post-TCJA, so §902 is irrelevant. (d) The supporting documents cite different baskets: the RAR says “general limitation basket under §904(d)(1)(A)” (that paragraph is the §951A category), and the reserve schedule says §904(d)(1)(B) (the foreign branch category). (e) The draft does not say whether the $2,310,000 of credits exceeding the limitation is permanently lost (the §951A basket has no carryover under §904(c)) or may be carried back one year and forward ten years (general basket). It also does not fix the resulting carryovers into 2023 and later years.",
evidence="RAR §IV.A–IV.B and §VII (FTC “TBD”); Marsh emails of Nov. 14 and Dec. 5, 2024; Voss emails of Nov. 22 and Dec. 18, 2024 (Salgado available for questions); Reserve schedule, FTC UTP tab; Draft §VI.",
risk="Ridgeline would be fixing, finally and permanently, a $2.31 million figure (plus its interest) that neither side has shown to be correct. Through the Section VI recitals it would also adopt a sourcing characterization that may prejudice its §904 positions in open years.",
fix="Before signing, obtain RA Salgado’s year-by-year §904 computation: baskets, foreign-source taxable income before and after, the limitation, credits claimed, and the treatment of excess credits. Have Mr. Patel and Pinnacle verify it. Attach it as a schedule to Exhibit C. Delete the §902 reference. Replace the sourcing narrative in Sections VI.A and VI.C with a neutral statement (“the parties have recomputed the Taxpayer’s foreign tax credit limitation under §904 to reflect the adjustments in Section IV, as set forth in Schedule C-1”). Add an express provision fixing any FTC carryover arising from the recomputation."),

dict(id="11", sev="High", cat="Substantive tax", prov="Section III.C; Section IX.C; new Section required",

dict(id="12", sev="High", cat="Substantive tax", prov="Section IV.D; Section V.D; Exhibit C Line 1",
title="Tax on the adjustments is computed at a flat 21% with no collateral or correlative adjustments (FDII, GILTI, §280C(c)/§174, credit limitations)",
issue="The draft taxes the full $104,960,000 at 21% and treats every credit dollar as a tax dollar. It ignores several known effects that may reduce the deficiency. (a) §250 FDII: royalty income from licensing IP for foreign use, including to a foreign related party whose products are sold to unrelated foreign customers, is generally foreign-derived deduction-eligible income. If Ridgeline claimed FDII on its as-filed returns, the incremental royalty should increase FDDEI. The theoretical ceiling is about $8.3 million (37.5% × $104.96M × 21%), subject to the taxable-income limitation and the DTIR computation. (b) §951A: the adjustment reduces RTIL’s tested income, which reduces Ridgeline’s GILTI inclusion and §960(d) credits. That interacts with Issue 9. (c) §280C(c): if Ridgeline did not make the reduced-credit election, it reduced its research deductions (for 2022, its §174 capital account) by the credits claimed. Disallowing $11,220,000 of credits should restore a corresponding deduction or amortization (up to about $2.36 million of tax at 21%, phased for 2022). (d) For 2022, if Phase IV costs are not §174 expenditures (as the IRS’s §41(d)(1)(A) position implies), they may be currently deductible under §162 instead of capitalized under amended §174. (e) If any credits were limited under §38(c) or carried forward, disallowance changes carryforwards rather than current tax.",
evidence="Draft §§IV.D, V.D, Exhibit C Footnote 1; RAR §III.C (four-part test begins with §174 requirement); Reserve schedule (“Credits are dollar-for-dollar tax benefits”); Hartwell & Stein §2 (licensed territory is all territories outside the U.S.).",
risk="Ridgeline may be agreeing to overpay by several million dollars. Section X.B bars later correction, and §7121(b) bars reopening.",
fix="Have Ridgeline’s tax department and Pinnacle run a full pro forma recomputation of each Covered Tax Year (FDII, GILTI, §78, §280C(c), §174, §38) on the settled terms before execution. Then either (i) state in Exhibit C that the deficiency reflects all correlative adjustments (and attach the Form 4549-style computation), or (ii) add: “The deficiencies set forth herein shall be adjusted to reflect all correlative and computational adjustments resulting from the Covered Issues, including under IRC §§78, 250, 280C(c), 904 and 951A.”"),

title="Finality clause is overbroad: it resolves “all federal income tax issues for tax years 2019 through 2022”",
issue="Form 906 is a closing agreement covering specific matters. evidence="Draft §§III.B–III.C; Letter 907 “Scope and Finality”; Voss email of Dec. 18, 2024 (“will cover only federal income tax liabilities for tax years 2019–2022 …”).",
risk="Could bar Ridgeline’s own affirmative claims for 2019–2022, such as refund claims, additional R&D credits, FTC or FDII positions, or carryback claims. It could also be read to fix items not actually negotiated. Ambiguity in a document that cannot be reopened is itself a material risk.",
fix="Revise Section III.C to read: “This Agreement is final and conclusive solely as to the Covered Issues for the Covered Tax Years. dict(id="16", sev="Medium", cat="Drafting", prov="Recital B; Section IV.E",
title="Recitals misdescribe the license and the benchmarking study",
issue="(a) Recital B says the 2016 License Agreement “was accompanied by a contemporaneous transfer pricing study.” In fact the Hartwell & Stein study is dated Nov. 15, 2018, more than two years after the license (effective July 1, 2016), with a March 2022 addendum. title="Corporate signatory and IRS signatory authority need to be confirmed",
issue="(a) Taxpayer: the signature block names Sandra Kwon, Tax Director. **PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL --- ATTORNEY-CLIENT COMMUNICATION / ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT**

**PEMBERTON HALE & GRIGGS LLP**

**MEMORANDUM**

**TO:** Eleanor Marsh, Partner

**CC:** David Yun, Senior Associate

**FROM:** Tax Controversy Team

**DATE:** January 2025 (prepared on review of the January 10, 2025 draft; response due February 7, 2025)

**CLIENT/MATTER:** Ridgeline Therapeutics, Inc. (EIN 47-3918205) --- IRS Case No. LBI-2023-0471-SD, Tax Years 2019--2022

**RE:** Issues Identified in Draft IRS Closing Agreement (Form 906) Transmitted Under Letter 907 --- Severity Ratings and Recommended Fixes

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# I. Executive Summary and Bottom Line

Recommendation: Ridgeline should not execute the draft Form 906 in its current form. Before the February 7, 2025 deadline we should send Appeals a written list of corrections and request a written extension. The draft records the negotiated terms correctly in its operative sections (16% royalty rate; 40% concession of disallowed Phase IV credits; \$2,310,000 FTC reduction; penalty abatement). But the payment computation that converts those terms into dollars is materially wrong, and several provisions Ridgeline needs are missing or drafted against its interests.

**Key points:**

- **Payment figure is understated by \$23.3 million.** Exhibit C subtracts the restored R&D credits (\$7,480,000) instead of adding the credits that remain disallowed (\$11,220,000), and subtracts the FTC reduction (\$2,310,000) instead of adding it. On the agreed terms, the amount due is \$39,311,600 using the IRS's interest figure, not \$15,991,600. The understatement is \$23,320,000 (Issues 1--3).

- **Two binding exhibits contradict the body.** Exhibit A transposes RTIL's 2020 net sales (\$578M instead of the RAR-verified \$587M). Exhibit B misstates the 2021 restored credit (\$1.6M instead of \$1.8M). Both exhibits are incorporated by reference, and nothing says whether the body or the exhibits control (Issues 4, 5, 15).

- **Interest of \$3,740,000 is unverifiable and appears materially understated.** Appeals has refused a year-by-year interest schedule. Ms. Voss's explanation that interest ran from "extended due date\[s\]" is legally incorrect (§6601(b)). Our estimate of statutory interest through March 1, 2025 is about \$7.9 million (\$8.5 million with §6621(c) hot interest), roughly double the stated figure. The draft nevertheless calls the \$3,740,000 a "final determination" (Issues 6--7).

- **Missing protective provisions with eight-figure consequences.** There is no Rev. Proc. 99-32 relief for the \$104.96 million of royalty RTIL never paid, no preservation of competent-authority correlative relief (Irish tax on the reallocated income is about \$13.1 million), and no reflection of correlative computational items (FDII, GILTI, §280C(c)/§174). The FTC figure has no supporting computation, and its rationale conflicts with §862(a)(4) (Issues 9--12).42
